content:
Maya: Quick heads-up — bringing up cascade-bert-embed-v2 on wiki-small holdout. After a deterministic seed rotation across microbatches I'm seeing cluster / recall jitter that looks larger than expected.

Maya: Baseline (seed=42) recall@1=0.783, recall@10=0.922. After seed swap (seed=31415) recall@1=0.742, recall@10=0.864. UMAP shows anchor clouds shift.

Rafa: Oof. Did you also change batching or any preprocessing?

Maya: No other changes. Same tokenizer, same PCA whitening. Only difference in the run was random seed and we re-shuffled the holdout before slicing for multi-batch eval.

Emma: Can you paste the eval command + the seed param you used? Also which quant path was this on (fp16 / int8)?

Maya: Sure — nascent experiment was fp16. Command:
```
./run_embed_eval --model cascade-bert-embed-v2 \\n  --dataset wiki-small-holdout \\n  --batch-size 256 \\n  --seed 31415 \\n  --metric recall@1,recall@10,ndcg
```

Jonas: Did you run full reruns with seed fixed across microbatches? Sometimes if the RNG differs in data-loader vs augmentation you'll see across-batch ordering effects that change KV cache behavior downstream.

Maya: I did a quick check: seed fixed at process level but each dataloader worker had worker_init_fn that used worker_seed = seed + worker_id. Could that explain it?

Rafa: Possibly. If microbatch alignment to sequence lengths changes, batching kernel selection can pick different kernels, causing minor float diff and eventual neighborhood movement.

Emma: Can you run two runs with identical global seed and force worker_seed to constant (e.g., seed + 0)? Also toggle shuffle off to test ordering.

Maya: Will do. Spawning two jobs now.

eval-bot: Job 4345678910 queued: run_embed_eval(cascade-bert-embed-v2,seed=31415,shuffle=true)

Maya: First job (shuffle=true) finished. Metrics: recall@1=0.745, recall@10=0.867 — small diff but still lower than baseline. UMAP shows same direction of drift for ~12% of anchors.

Maya: Second job (shuffle=false, worker_seed=seed) finished. Metrics: recall@1=0.781, recall@10=0.919 — very close to baseline.

Rafa: That suggests ordering/shuffle interacting with microbatching is the main factor. Good catch.

Emma: Next step: try int8 quant path with deterministic worker seeds + shuffle=false. If quantization amplifies numeric drift we'll want to quantify worst-case recall drop and add as regression test.

Jonas: For regression tests, capture anchor-level id lists for seeds 42 and 31415 and compute per-anchor rank delta. We should set an alert if >5% anchors move by >k positions for recall@10 targets.

Maya: I'll produce a small diff table and push artifacts (umap plots + id-deltas). Also adding a short note to the model onboarding checklist: "ensure deterministic eval runs — control worker_seed + shuffle when comparing model variants".

Rafa: Nice. Can you also add a quick script to re-run with multiple fixed seeds (42, 31415, 271828) to estimate seed-sensitivity distribution? Keep n=3 to be cheap.

Maya: Yep — will run the 3-seed sweep with both fp16 and int8 and upload results by EOD.

Emma: Thanks — once we have int8 numbers we can decide whether to mark the quantization profile as safe or require per-customer opt-in. :thumbsup:

Maya: Uploaded artifacts to the eval bucket: s3://redwood-evals/cascade-bert-v2/seed-rotation/{umap,recall-deltas,run-manifests}. Will link in the PR.

Jonas: TL;DR: seed + shuffle can create ordering that interacts with batching/kernel selection; deterministic eval harness and small seed-sweep recommended before marking model as onboarded.

Maya: Agreed. Filing a short follow-up doc in the onboarding repo with reproducer and recommended flags.

Rafa: Thanks — great triage.
